title: Canvas: pick the substrate - Excalidraw embed vs tldraw vs custom
description:
Blocks the contract ticket, because the scene schema falls out of this choice.

THE PROPOSAL says 'Excalidraw-style', not 'Excalidraw'. That wording is
deliberate - it describes the feel (hand-drawn, low-ceremony, fast) and leaves
the implementation open.

WHAT THE CHOICE HAS TO SATISFY (all from the proposal):
  - Human draws arrays, pointers, trees, recursion stacks, state tables, arrows
  - Agent can READ the scene as structured data
  - Agent can WRITE into the scene - annotations in its own colour
  - Snapshots are replayable as a timeline
  - Must also serve the later system-design and incident tracks, which are
    box-and-arrow heavy rather than data-structure heavy

CANDIDATES:
  Excalidraw    - MIT, mature, the aesthetic the proposal names, well-documented
                  element format, programmatic API for injecting elements.
                  Heaviest bundle. Check the collaboration/multiplayer story if
                  human and agent edit concurrently.
  tldraw        - excellent editor API and shape model, strong programmatic
                  control. Licence is NOT plain open source - verify current
                  terms against intended use before committing.
  custom        - full control, no licence questions, exactly the primitives
                  needed. Weeks of work to reach usable, and hand-drawn feel is
                  hard to fake.

RECOMMENDATION TO EVALUATE, NOT ASSUME: Excalidraw embed. It is what the
proposal gestures at, its element JSON is a ready-made agent contract, and
injecting agent-authored elements is a solved problem in its API.

DELIVERABLE: a short written decision with the licence position stated
explicitly, plus a spike proving the agent can inject an element and read the
scene back.

NOTE: there is an excalidraw-diagram skill on this machine that emits Excalidraw
JSON, and an archify skill for diagram rendering. Both are prior art worth
reading before choosing - the JSON shapes are already understood locally.

title: Canvas <-> agent contract: scene JSON + rendered PNG dual representation
description:
Phase 0 spec deliverable (proposal section 9, week 1). Blocks everything else on the canvas.

WHAT THE PROPOSAL SPECIFIES:
  'Agent reads the canvas as structured scene JSON plus a rendered PNG (vision)'

Two representations, both needed, for different reasons:
  - SCENE JSON  - precise, addressable, diffable. Lets the agent reason about
                  specific elements, reference them by id, and write annotations
                  that attach to them.
  - PNG         - vision input. Handles the things structure loses: spatial
                  relationships, sloppy handwriting, an arrow that 'points at'
                  something without being bound to it.

WHAT MUST BE DECIDED AND WRITTEN DOWN:
  1. The scene schema the agent sees. If Excalidraw is the substrate, its
     element format is the obvious candidate - but decide whether the agent gets
     raw Excalidraw elements or a normalised projection. Raw is cheaper and
     lossless; normalised is stabler against upstream changes and much smaller
     in tokens.
  2. When the agent gets a snapshot. Every stroke is too noisy and too
     expensive. On request? On a debounce? On stage transition? This is a cost
     and latency decision as much as a design one.
  3. How the agent addresses an element it wants to annotate or critique -
     stable ids, and what happens when the human deletes an element the agent
     referenced.
  4. Token budget. A dense recursion-stack drawing could produce a large scene
     payload. Decide the truncation/summarisation rule before it bites.
  5. Coordinate space and units, so agent-authored elements land where intended.

ACCEPTANCE: a written contract doc in this repo that a canvas implementation and
an agent implementation could be built against independently.

DEPENDS ON: the tool decision (Excalidraw vs tldraw vs custom) - the schema
follows from it.

title: Shared canvas: Excalidraw-style whiteboard both human and agent see and edit
description:
PARENT TICKET. Source: algopeeps-product-proposal.md section 6 'Shared canvas'. The proposal holds the argument; this repo holds the task list.

THE PITCH (verbatim from the proposal):
  An Excalidraw-style whiteboard both human and agent see and edit. Purpose: make
  stage 2 (PLAN) a real whiteboarding step rather than a text box. Interviews
  happen on whiteboards; prep tools don't have one.

  - Human draws arrays, pointers, trees, recursion stacks, state tables, arrows.
  - Agent reads the canvas as structured scene JSON plus a rendered PNG (vision)
    and can add annotations in its own colour: circle a mistake, add a
    counterexample input, label an invariant.
  - Canvas snapshots are session events, so a post-mortem can replay the drawing
    timeline.
  - The canvas is also the primary surface for the later system-design and
    incident tracks.

WHY IT MATTERS / THE DIFFERENTIATOR:
Real interviews happen on whiteboards. No existing prep tool has one that an
agent can actually read and draw on. This is the interaction layer that makes
algopeeps something other than a chat box with a code editor attached.

WHERE IT SITS IN THE PRACTICE LOOP (proposal section 6):
  1 CLASSIFY -> 2 PLAN -> 3 CODE -> 4 LOOK BACK -> 5 PROVE IT (>=7 days later)

  Stage 2 PLAN is 'canvas + invariant + complexity before any code'.
  Stage 3 CODE 'unlocks only after plan is accepted'.

So the canvas is not a side feature - it is load-bearing for the core product
claim that the tutor structurally cannot hand you the answer. The gate between
PLAN and CODE runs through it.

PHASING (proposal section 9):
  Phase 0, week 1:      'canvas <-> agent contract' is a named spec deliverable
  Phase 1, weeks 4-6:   'shared canvas' ships in the dogfood build

CHILDREN: see linked issues for the contract, the annotation layer, snapshot
events, the tool decision, and the PLAN->CODE gate.

NOTE ON HISTORY: beads issues existed in this repo from 2026-01-03 ('Add
Algopeeps Council v0 plan and beads issue tracking') but lived in the embedded
Dolt DB, which beads gitignores. That DB died with the local clone in the
2026-09-17 machine migration and was never exported to .beads/issues.jsonl, so
any earlier canvas tickets are unrecoverable. These are filed fresh from the
proposal. Remember to run 'bd export -o .beads/issues.jsonl' and commit it.

title: Canvas gates the PLAN -> CODE transition
description:
The canvas is load-bearing for the product's core claim. Depends on the annotation layer.

WHAT THE PROPOSAL SPECIFIES (practice loop, section 6):
  Stage 2 PLAN:  'canvas + invariant + complexity before any code'
  Stage 3 CODE:  'unlocks only after plan is accepted'

So the editor is literally locked until a plan on the canvas is accepted. That
makes the canvas the enforcement point for the whole thesis - an AI tutor that
is 'structurally unable to give away answers'.

WHAT HAS TO BE DECIDED:
  1. WHAT 'ACCEPTED' MEANS. The human draws an approach and states an invariant
     plus complexity. Something has to judge that it is coherent enough to
     proceed. Too strict and it is infuriating; too loose and the gate is
     theatre. This is the hardest design problem in the ticket.
  2. WHO JUDGES. An LLM grading against a rubric is the obvious answer and
     matches understanding metric 3 (SOLO level, LLM-graded). But the judge must
     not leak the solution while rejecting a plan - same constraint as the
     annotation layer.
  3. WHAT A REJECTION LOOKS LIKE. Rejection must teach without solving. The
     counterexample-input annotation is the natural vehicle: do not say 'your
     plan is wrong', draw the input that breaks it.
  4. THE ESCAPE HATCH. The struggle timer is 20-45 min and the help ladder is
     policy-capped. What happens when someone is stuck at the gate past the
     timer? Ladder rungs presumably escalate until the plan is reachable - but
     the policy must be written, not improvised.
  5. Does an accepted plan get frozen as the reference for stage 4 LOOK BACK,
     so the post-mortem can compare intent against what was actually coded?

RISK: this gate is where the product is most likely to feel hostile rather than
rigorous. Worth dogfooding early and tuning hard - proposal Phase 1 kill
criterion is 'author stops using it after 2 weeks'.

title: Canvas snapshots as replayable session events
description:
Depends on the contract. Makes the canvas evidence rather than scratch.

WHAT THE PROPOSAL SPECIFIES:
  'Canvas snapshots are session events, so a post-mortem can replay the drawing
   timeline.'

WHY THIS IS MORE THAN A NICE-TO-HAVE:
Stage 4 of the practice loop is LOOK BACK - 'name the cue, the pattern, what
failed'. You cannot do that honestly from memory. The drawing timeline is the
record of how the plan actually evolved: what was drawn first, what was erased,
where the human stalled, when the agent intervened and what happened next.

It also feeds the understanding metrics (proposal section 6):
  metric 4 - 'time to first correct plan' is measurable directly off this timeline
  metric 5 - 'hint rung used' - canvas annotations are rungs, so they belong on
             the same timeline as text hints

DESIGN QUESTIONS:
  1. Snapshot granularity. Per-stroke is faithful but heavy. Debounced diffs
     against the last snapshot are probably the right shape - store deltas, not
     full scenes, with periodic keyframes.
  2. Event schema. Canvas events should sit in the SAME session event stream as
     hint requests, stage transitions and code submissions - not a separate
     store. Otherwise the post-mortem cannot interleave 'they drew this, then
     asked for a hint, then erased it'.
  3. Retention. A dogfood build can keep everything; decide before that stops
     being true.
  4. Replay UI. Scrubbable timeline. Probably Phase 2 (self-instrumentation)
     rather than Phase 1, but the EVENTS must be captured from Phase 1 or the
     data is gone forever.

CRITICAL SEQUENCING: capture the events in Phase 1 even if replay UI lands in
Phase 2. Instrumentation that is not recorded from the start cannot be
backfilled.

title: Canvas: agent annotation layer with colour ownership
description:
The agent's half of the shared canvas. Depends on the contract and the substrate choice.

WHAT THE PROPOSAL SPECIFIES:
  'can add annotations in its own colour: circle a mistake, add a counterexample
   input, label an invariant'

Three named annotation kinds, each tied to the pedagogy rather than being
generic drawing:
  CIRCLE A MISTAKE      - point at a specific element the human drew and mark it
                          wrong, WITHOUT saying what the fix is. This is the
                          product's core constraint: the tutor structurally
                          cannot give away the answer.
  COUNTEREXAMPLE INPUT  - add a concrete input that breaks the drawn plan. The
                          strongest form of feedback that is not a solution.
  LABEL AN INVARIANT    - name the thing the human's drawing implies but did not
                          state. Feeds understanding metric 3 (explanation
                          quality, SOLO level of the stated invariant).

DESIGN CONSTRAINTS:
  - COLOUR OWNERSHIP IS NOT COSMETIC. The learner must always be able to tell
    what they reasoned versus what the agent supplied - otherwise stage 5
    (cold re-solve >=7 days later) is measuring the agent's work, not theirs.
    Agent-authored elements need a durable owner field in the scene, not just a
    colour that a human could accidentally reuse.
  - Agent annotations must be separable: hideable for a cold re-solve, and
    visible in the post-mortem replay.
  - Annotation volume must be policy-capped. See the help ladder in the
    proposal - help is rationed, attempt required between rungs, struggle timer
    20-45 min. An agent that freely annotates would route around the ladder
    entirely. Drawing on the canvas IS a help rung and must be accounted as one.

OPEN QUESTION worth settling early: does an agent annotation consume a hint rung
from the same budget as a text hint, or is there a separate canvas budget?
